catalog_quote: Because vowels are not reduced in unstressed position, CC is a syllable timed language, like Spanish or French, rather than stress timed like English. ... Intonation. The pitch contours of CC are very similar to those of Creole French. High pitch marks stress; low pitch is non-stress. Certain elements within a sentence, such as the nucleus of a noun or verb phrase, must carry high pitch. Other emelents, such as the preclitics for aspect, are nearly always unstressed. In a noun or noun phrase of more than one syllable, stress tends to fall on the last syllable unless the nucleus of the last syllable is /l/, which cannot be stressed.. Note the following (stressed sylllable is in CAPS): /man-GO/ 'mango' /si-KYAT/ 'octopus' /gyad-N/ 'garden' /kom-fo-TE-bl/ 'comfortable' /KYAN-dl/ 'candle'

new_statements.rule_in_words: In polysyllabic nouns (and noun phrases) stress, realised as high pitch, falls on the last syllable; a final syllabic /l/ cannot bear stress, so in such words stress lands on the preceding syllable (man-GÓ, si-KYÁT, gyad-Ń, but KYÁN-dl, kom-fo-TÉ-bl). Vowels are not reduced in unstressed syllables (syllable-timed). Kephart 2000 (snippet, not opened) restates this as 'Word stress placement is predictable and right-anchored in CCE'.
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllable whose nucleus is syllabic /l/ cannot be stressed (stress retracts one syllable); the rule is stated for nouns/NPs and hedged with 'tends to'; at sentence level NP/VP nuclei must carry high pitch while aspect preclitics are nearly always unstressed, and the prenucleics /bin/ (anterior) and /kyan-/ are stressed, i.e. carry high pitch (pp. 82, 84). Kephart's snippet-only chapter 'Bilingual aspects of language in a Creole community' adds 'Stress is not phonemic at the word level'.
new_statements.domain_note: Placement rule stated for 'a noun or noun phrase of more than one syllable' (word/NP level); the pitch statements are sentence-level; examples are isolated citation-form words. Author's own analysis of Carriacou Creole English ('CC'), sketch-level ('intended as a sketch only', p. 62).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Carriacou Creole English ('CC'/'CCE'), the creole of Carriacou island (Carriacou & Petite Martinique dependency of Grenada), which Glottolog subsumes under gren1247 Grenadian Creole English (no separate glottocode). Whether Grenada-island and Carriacou creoles are one variety was raised by Holbrook 2005 (not opened); treat the rule as attested for the Carriacou variety.

III 'System and Contrast', section 'Phonology' (pp. 62-70), subsections 'Syllables and Timing' and 'Intonation' p. 70, examples p. 71: CC is syllable-timed (no vowel reduction); high pitch marks stress, low pitch non-stress; in a noun/NP of more than one syllable stress tends to fall on the last syllable unless its nucleus is syllabic /l/, which cannot be stressed (man-GO, si-KYAT, gyad-N vs KYAN-dl, kom-fo-TE-bl); NP/VP nuclei must carry high pitch, aspect preclitics are nearly always unstressed; /bin/ and /kyan-/ are stressed prenucleics (pp. 82, 84).
